The post Bland Launches Tofu-1, a Full-Duplex Speech-to-Speech Model for Calls appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Bland, the San Francisco voice-AI company, has released Tofu-1 , a full-duplex speech-to-speech model in research preview. The Tofu-1 speech-to-speech model targets calls from moving cars, hospital rooms and weak-signal lines. It listens while it speaks and reasons while it talks. For phone-agent teams, one model now handles audio in and audio out, with no transcript between. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . What is Tofu-1? Tofu-1 is a full-duplex speech-to-speech model from Bland that hears, reasons and replies in audio during phone calls. It is the first release in a planned family of Bland speech-to-speech models. How does Tofu-1 differ from a cascade voice agent? Most voice agents are cascades. They turn speech into text, pass it to a language model, then turn the reply back into speech. Tofu-1 listens to the audio directly , so tone, hesitation and background sound stay available to the model. Bland has not published the internal architecture. Audio understanding Bland lists 3 audio skills on its product page: Speaker tracking: tells speakers apart and works out who each one is addressing. Noise separation: separates voices from a crying child, a TV, highway traffic, a hospital intercom or keypad tones. Paralinguistics: hears hesitation, frustration and urgency. Full duplex and thinking while talking Callers can interrupt or correct Tofu-1 mid-sentence. While it works on a request, it keeps the conversation moving. It reports the result only when the work is done. It never claims a task is finished early. Scene generation Because Tofu-1 models the sound of a call, it can also produce one. That includes a second speaker, the room around them and line noise. What is Bland’s ‘TV Test’? The TV Test asks one question: can the model follow the caller while ignoring speech from another scene? TV audio is often louder than the caller. Bland marks its TV Test walkthrough as illustrative, not recorded model output. How does Tofu-1 compare with other full-duplex models? FDB results use different benchmark versions and are not directly comparable. How can teams access Tofu-1? Research preview access is open to a limited number of enterprises. Bland names banking, healthcare, insurance and government as target sectors. The sign-up form asks for monthly call volume, from under 1,000 to 50,000+. Key Takeaways Tofu-1 is Bland’s first full-duplex speech-to-speech model, built for noisy calls. It hears audio directly: speakers, background noise and caller emotion. The only number is self-reported: over 92% could not spot it in screenings. No size, latency, pricing or benchmarks yet; rivals publish latency and tool-use scores. Access is a closed enterprise preview, with Bland citing January availability. Check out the Tofu-1 product page , the launch post on X and the research preview sign-up . The post Cmpnd Releases dspy-wsp: Weight-Space Programming Comes to DSPy appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Cmpnd has released dspy-wsp , a prototype optimizer that brings weight-space programming to DSPy . Weight-space programming is a technique in which a frontier LLM reads another model’s weights and edits them directly. There are no gradients, no training loop and no fine-tuning dataset. dspy-wsp packages this as WeightSpace , an optimizer that plugs into any DSPy program and metric. In Cmpnd’s tests, about $5 to $10 of GPT-6-Astra calls improved every decision model they tried. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR What it is: A DSPy optimizer ( WeightSpace ) where a writer LLM edits a student model’s weights. MIT license, pip install dspy-wsp , needs DSPy 3.5. Size: Tested on open decision models from 0.6B to 9B parameters. One 25-pass run edited a single layer or head. Runs on: One Mac for all experiments. 2B models used about 6 GB of memory. d1-omni-600M needs 4 GB or more (Mac or GPU). Performance: WeightSpace alone added 1.9 to 16.1 points on Typed Decisions. With ReAnchor, gains were 6.5 to 20.0 points. Best: d1-omni-600M rose from 50.9% to 69.1% (+18.3) with WeightSpace + ReAnchor. Worst: Clef-Flash (9B) gained only +1.9 from WeightSpace alone. With the original paper’s stricter rule, d1-omni-600M gained just +2.8. Bottom line: Best: a cheap, gradient-free edit that ships as a small, verifiable patch. Worst: very experimental, slow (78 to 167 minutes per run) and weakest on larger models. What is weight-space programming? Weight-space programming (WSP) treats a neural network’s weights as a program that can be read and rewritten. The idea comes from MIT research: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming . A frontier model (the research team used GPT-6-Astra) looks at weight tensors, reasons about what each part computes, and changes them to match a goal written in plain English. The research team stresses that WSP names an emerging capability, not a fixed method. Gradients were banned in their experiments, but the concept does not rule them out.
